fixes.explanation: Good guess, but David never says a word about gates. What he says is that Absalom “…will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” His plan is to flee, and to leave quickly.

I see why you'd think it, since the messenger just said the hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom. But that's not what David says will happen. His warning is about Absalom himself: “…he will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.”

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: “Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him.” His household goes with him. The ones he leaves behind are ten concubines, to take care of the palace.
That's right. “Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him.” That's the whole household on the move. He does leave ten concubines behind to take care of the palace.
Gates is a fair guess, but the text says he left the ten concubines behind “…to take care of the palace.” The gates aren't mentioned in that verse at all. The job is the palace.

That's the one, baker. Ittai says, “…wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” Remember, David had just told him he was a foreigner who arrived only yesterday.

David tells him to go back and stay with the new king, but that's not what Ittai says. Ittai answers with a promise to stay: “…wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” He doesn't take the exit.
Yes, baker. After Ittai's promise, David says, “March on then…” and Ittai marches past with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. David gave the man a way out and he didn't take it.
No beach day on this trip, baker. The text says that as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, the people passed “…toward the way of the wilderness.” No sea is mentioned anywhere in the verse.
That's not what David says in this verse. He says, “then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” There's no battle plan in it. His words are about leaving the decision to the LORD.

David doesn't announce any big exit here. He says, “then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” That's a king leaving the outcome to the LORD. Just before this, he says that if he finds favor in the eyes of the LORD, “He will bring me back…”

You got it, baker. David tells Zadok, the priest, “…I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.” He sends the priests back to Jerusalem and says he'll wait at the fords for their word. That's a lot of trust sent back down the road.

It's actually true, baker. The text says, “…all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.” David wasn't the only one covering his head. The people with him covered theirs too.

Yes, baker. Ahithophel is the counselor who is now among Absalom's conspirators, and David pleads, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” Notice where he takes the news: straight to the LORD.
Hushai is sent to the city, but guarding the palace isn't the job. David says, “…you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city…” This is more of a mission than a post.

You got it, baker. David says the priests' two sons, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar, are there with them, and tells Hushai, “Send them to me with everything you hear.” So David's plan is for the news to go from Hushai to the priests, then out with the two sons. That's a three-stop delivery route.
